exclude: the ROM, or the language card's RAM
the line buffer GETLN fills and the interpreter prints from, and the Z-machine's stack, which grows down from $03E7 (runtime state)

the text screen, which at the Z-machine's start holds only spaces and the `Apple //e` line the ROM printed at power-on, and its screen holes, where the disk routines keep each drive's head position ($0478, $04F8) (not the game's)
the four tables of which story page is in which buffer, built at start-up over the loader (runtime state)
the disk routines' nibble buffers, holding whatever sector was read last (runtime state)
the story's first $48 pages, read from the disk at start-up and kept, which the 6502 code reaches only through the Z-machine's addresses: the story's own, listed with the story (parts/story)
the 76 page buffers, filled from the disk as the story needs its pages (runtime state; empty at the Z-machine's start)

comments.text: Not a variable: the address the start-up loop at $0805 indexes, STA $00,X with X from $80 to $FF, to clear the interpreter's half of zero page. $00-$1F themselves are never read or written by the interpreter.
The Monitor's text window, left edge. The interpreter sets it to 0 at $1D94 when it sets up the screen.

The Monitor's window width, 40, set at $1D98. The output routine at $1B90 wraps its line at this column, and the [MORE] code at $1C5B compares the line length with it to decide whether a carriage return is needed.
The Monitor's window top, set to 1 at $1D90 so that HOME and scrolling leave line 0, the status line, alone. The line counter at $ED restarts from it after each input line and each [MORE].
The Monitor's window bottom, 24, set at $1D9C. When the count of lines printed since the last input ($ED) reaches it, $1C5B shows [MORE].

The Monitor's cursor column. The status line code at $1CD7 saves it, draws at column 0 and then column 25, and puts it back; [MORE] at $1C5B moves it back six places to rub the prompt out; the save prompts set it to 25 for the default answer.
The Monitor's cursor row, saved and restored round the status line at $1CD7, which draws on row 0.

Disk routines' work byte: the first byte of the secondary buffer held while a sector is written ($2438), the index into the buffers while one is read ($2502), the byte count of a partial sector ($24D7), and the number of steps taken while the head moves ($25AB).

Disk routines' work byte: the slot times 16 while a sector is written ($242B), the running checksum of an address field as it is read ($256F-$2583), and the track the head starts from while it moves ($25B0).
The track position the seek routine at $25A0 is moving the head to, in half tracks.
The slot times 16 that the seek routine at $25A0 steps, kept so that it can index the phase switches $C080-$C087 by slot.
The four bytes of the last address field the disk routines read ($2544): $2C the checksum, $2D the sector, $2E the track, $2F the volume, stored by STA $002C,Y with Y counting down from 3.
The sector number of the last address field read, compared with the sector wanted after translation through the table at $2BB8 ($2A2B).
The track number of the last address field read; $29ED compares it with the track the head is supposed to be on and seeks again if it differs.
The volume number of the last address field read, copied into the parameter block's byte $0E ($2A15) and checked against the volume asked for, when one was.

The Monitor's inverse flag: $3F prints in inverse, $FF normally. The interpreter sets $3F for the status line ($1CE9), [MORE] ($1C6D) and the default answers of the save prompts ($1F92), and $FF again after each.
The Monitor's prompt character, set to $3E, `>`, at $1DA0. GETLN1, which the interpreter calls to read a line, does not print it itself.
Disk routines' flag: bit 7 says which drive is selected ($2A9B, $297F), so the routines keep each drive's track in its own screen hole.

The Monitor's output hook, low byte. The printer routine at $1BF2 swaps it with the interpreter's printer hook at $EE-$EF, sends its text through COUT, and swaps back, so the screen's hook is restored after each line sent to the printer; new_line does the same at $1CA3 to send the printer its carriage return.
The Monitor's output hook, high byte, swapped with $EF in the same way as $36, at $1BF2 and at $1CA3.

A false symbol: $38 is the operand of BIT $38 at $2A47 in the disk routines, a skip over the SEC at $2A48 (opcode $38) that the error exits jump to. The interpreter never uses the input hook KSW here, and $39-$3B are not used.
The address of the device characteristics table, copied from bytes 6-7 of the parameter block at $2954 (the table at $1DBD). $3D is its high byte.

The address of the 256-byte buffer a sector is read into or written from, copied from bytes 8-9 of the parameter block at $2954; $3F is its high byte. The pre-nibble and post-nibble routines at $2400 and $24C2 index it.
High byte of the sector buffer's address. The format routine at $2AAF uses $3F as the sector number it is writing ($2B0D).
The volume number the format routine writes into each address field it makes ($2AB3, $2888).
The track the format routine is writing, counting from 0 to 34 ($2ABD-$2AFD), also written into each address field ($288D).
The number of sync bytes the format routine writes between sectors; it starts at 40 ($2AD0) and is adjusted at $2B52-$2BA4 so that sixteen sectors fit the track.
A 16-bit count the delay routine at $2600 increments, used at $299E to wait out the drive motor's start-up time from the device characteristics table.
High byte of the motor start-up count ($46), loaded at $2962 from the fourth byte of the device characteristics table, $D8.
The address of the RWTS parameter block (IOB) the disk routines were called with: Y and A at $2900 go to $48-$49. On the Apple II $48 is also where the Monitor keeps P.
High byte of the parameter block's address, stored at $2902; the interpreter always passes $1DAC.

The Monitor's random number, low byte, counted up while the Monitor waits for a key. The interpreter's random number routine at $21E8 reads it with $4F, so a random result depends on how long the player took to type. $50-$7B are not used by the interpreter.
The Monitor's random number, high byte. $21E8 rotates it left with the carry each time it is read, so two random numbers asked for in one turn differ.

A routine in zero page that the dispatcher calls before every Z-machine instruction ($0A2E, JSR $007C). The loader puts an RTS ($60) here at $232F and nothing else writes it, so the call does nothing; $7D-$7E are left free for a JMP that someone could put there to watch each instruction.
The number of sectors to a track, 16, set by the loader at $2333 and read by $1DD3, which turns a page number of the story or the save into a track and a sector.
The opcode byte of the Z-machine instruction being executed, read at $09AF; the decoders at $0A4B and $0A86 take the operand types from its bits, and $0AB6, $0A6E and $0A11 the operation number.
The number of operands decoded for the current instruction: 1 for a short form, 2 for a long form, 0-4 for a variable form. call and je read it.

The current instruction's operands, four 16-bit words at $82-$89, each low byte first: $82-$83 the first, $84-$85 the second, $86-$87 the third and $88-$89 the fourth. Every opcode handler takes its inputs from here.
High byte of the first operand.
Low byte of the second operand.
High byte of the second operand.
Low byte of the third operand: the value storew, storeb ($12AD) and put_prop write, and the third value je compares with ($1189).
High byte of the third operand.
Low byte of the fourth operand, which only je and call read.
High byte of the fourth operand.

The Z-machine's program counter, 17 bits in three bytes: $8A the offset within a 256-byte page of the story, $8B the page, $8C the top bit of the page number. The next byte of code is fetched from here by $1752.
The page of the story the program counter is in, the middle byte of the program counter.
The top bit of the program counter's page number, so that code can lie anywhere in 128K; the branch code at $0C37 keeps only bit 0.
The address in memory of the page the program counter is in, while $8F says it is valid; $8D is always 0 and $8E the page's high byte, so ($8D),Y with Y = $8A fetches the next byte.
High byte of the memory address of the program counter's page: a resident page ($2C-$73) or a buffer ($74-$BF).

$FF while $8D-$8E point at the program counter's page, 0 when the next fetch must look the page up again: cleared when the fetch crosses a page, after every backward jump or branch and every forward one into another page ($0C3D), a call, a return, a restore, and when the page's buffer is reused for another page. print and print_ret copy the string reader's own flag, $96, into it ($0C7C).
The buffer that holds the program counter's page, when that page is not resident: an index from 0 into the 76 buffers at $7400. $184B compares it with the buffer a data read is about to reuse.
The page part of the address that data reads come from ($1801): strings, words and bytes the Z-machine reads by address. $91 is the page, $92 its top bit and $93 the offset in the page.
The top bit of the data address's page number.
The offset within its page of the next byte a data read will fetch.
The memory address of the data address's page while $96 says it is valid; $94 is 0 and $95 the page's high byte.
High byte of the memory address of the data page.
$FF while $94-$95 point at the data address's page, 0 when the next data read must look its page up.
The buffer that holds the data address's page when that page is not resident. $179C compares it with the buffer a code fetch is about to reuse.
The address in memory of the Z-machine's global variables, header word $0C plus the story's base, set at $08E1. Global variable n is at $98 + 2(n - 16), high byte first.
High byte of the address of the global variables ($4C with this story).

The current routine's local variables, fifteen 16-bit words at $9A-$B7, each high byte first: local n at $9A + 2(n - 1). call ($11A8) saves the caller's on the Z-machine's stack and ret ($0DFF) puts them back.
The address of the first page buffer: $B8 is 0 and $B9 the page after the story's resident part, $74. Buffer n is at ($B9 + n) * 256.
High byte of the first page buffer's address, the story's base plus the resident page count ($0901).
The address in memory where the story begins, $2C00: every Z-machine address of the resident part is this plus the address. The header is read through ($BA),Y.
High byte of the story's base address, $2C.

The number of the story's pages kept in memory for good, header byte 4 plus 1, $48 with this story: every page below this is read straight from $2C00 onwards, every page from it on goes through the buffers.
The number of page buffers, from the top of RAM ($1B6F) less the first buffer's page, plus one: 76 on a 48K machine, 12 on a 32K one.
The buffer used most recently, the head of the chain of buffers in order of use that $1880 keeps.
The buffer used least recently, the one the next page read from disk will replace ($18CB).
The address of the table at $2200 that holds, for each buffer, the low byte of the page number it holds.
High byte of the address of the page-number table, $22.
The address of the table at $2280 that holds, for each buffer, the top bit of the page number it holds.
High byte of the address of the second page-number table, $22.
The address of the table at $2300: for each buffer, the next buffer older in use, $FF for the oldest.
High byte of the address of the older-link table, $23.
The address of the table at $2380: for each buffer, the next buffer newer in use, $FF for the newest.
High byte of the address of the newer-link table, $23.
The number of words on the Z-machine's stack, plus one: it starts at 1 ($081B); a push past $B3 ($172C) or a pop down to 0 ($174A) is a fatal error.
The Z-machine's stack pointer, starting at $03E8 and growing down two bytes a push ($1708); the word at ($C9) is the top, high byte first.
High byte of the Z-machine's stack pointer.
The stack pointer when the current routine began, after its saved locals: ret ($0DFF) drops back to here, discarding whatever the routine left on the stack. $CC is its high byte.
High byte of the current routine's frame pointer.
The stack count ($C8) when the current routine began, restored by ret with $CB-$CC.
The alphabet that the next character of the string being printed comes from after a single shift (0 lower case, 1 upper case, 2 punctuation), or $FF when no shift is pending ($19CD consumes it).
The alphabet the string being printed is locked in, changed by the shift-lock characters 4 and 5; 0 at the start of each string. The word encoder at $1A25 uses it for the alphabet it has shifted to.
Which of the three 5-bit characters of the current word the string decoder takes next ($19D9): 0, 1 or 2, or $FF once the word with the end bit has been used up.
The low byte of the 16-bit word of the string being printed, three characters packed in it.
The high byte of the string's current word; bit 7 set marks the string's last word.

The characters of the word being parsed, up to six at $D3-$D8, cleared before each word ($1341); characters after the sixth are skipped ($13CD), which is why the game knows its words by their first six letters.
Set to $FF at start-up ($0829) and never read.

The encoded word the dictionary search compares: the encoder at $1A25 first writes six 5-bit characters at $DA-$DF, then $1B3C packs them into two words, $DA-$DB and $DC-$DD, low byte first, with the end bit set in $DD.
The high byte of the first word of the encoded word, compared first by the dictionary search ($145F, $149B).
The low byte of the second word of the encoded word.
The high byte of the second word of the encoded word, with bit 7 set.
The fifth 5-bit character before packing.
The sixth 5-bit character before packing.
The offset in the parse buffer of the entry the next word will fill: 2 for the first, then four more for each word ($13B5).
The offset in the text buffer of the next character the parser reads; 1 for the first, since byte 0 is the buffer's size.
The address in memory of the table of 32 abbreviations, header word $18 plus the story's base ($08EF).
High byte of the abbreviation table's address.
A 16-bit work register at $E4-$E5, used by nearly every routine: the second number of a sum, a divisor, a remainder, an address.
High byte of the work register at $E4.
The interpreter's main 16-bit register at $E6-$E7: the value an operand fetch returns, an opcode's result before it is stored, an object's address, the word pushed and popped.
High byte of the main work register at $E6.
A 16-bit work register at $E8-$E9: a count, a bit mask, the multiplier's partial product.
High byte of the work register at $E8, and the parser's count of characters left in the line.
The number of negative operands $160F made positive for a multiply or divide; if it is odd, $161E negates the result. The restore code also keeps the header's flags byte here.
The number of characters in the output line at $0200 that are waiting to be shown, which is also the column the next one goes in.
Where the output routine broke a line that was too long ($1BC1): the space it found, or the window width.
Lines printed since the player last typed: after each input line and each [MORE] it restarts from the window's top, and $1C5B shows [MORE] when it reaches the window's bottom.

The printer's output hook, $C100 (slot 1) from start-up: $1BF2 swaps it into CSW to print a line on the printer, and $1CA3 to print a carriage return, and each keeps whatever the printer card left in CSW for next time.
High byte of the printer's output hook, $C1.
A copy of the program counter at the start of each Z-machine instruction, made at $099F; nothing in the interpreter reads it. $F3-$FF after it are not used.
The page byte of the copy of the program counter made at $099F.
The top bit of the copy of the program counter made at $099F.

The interpreter's entry, where the loader jumps, and where RESTART and a disk error come back to. It clears zero page $80-$FF, resets the 6502 stack, points the printer hook at slot 1 ($C100), empties the Z-machine's stack (count 1, pointer $03E8), and builds the four 128-byte tables at $2200-$23FF that record which story page is in which buffer and the order the buffers were used in (every page number 0, each buffer linked to its neighbours, buffer 0 the newest). It sets up the screen ($1E36), reads page 0 of the story to $2C00, replaces header byte 5 with $FF, and reads the rest of the resident pages (header byte 4 plus 1, $48 pages) to $2C00-$73FF. A disk error at any read starts the whole thing again from here.

Checks the story's header and sets the Z-machine going: if bit 0 of header byte 1 is set the interpreter stops with its fatal error ($091E). It sets the program counter from header word 6, the globals pointer from word $0C and the abbreviation pointer from word $18, puts the first buffer straight after the resident pages ($7400), finds the top of RAM ($1B6F) and makes one buffer of every page from there down to $7400 (76 on a 48K machine), the last of them the oldest. Less than one page free is the fatal error. Then it jumps to the instruction loop at $099F ($091B), past the dispatch tables.
The fatal error for a story the interpreter cannot run: JSR $21E7, a BRK, so the machine drops into the Monitor.

The handlers of the twelve Z-machine instructions with no operands, opcodes $B0-$BB, in order: rtrue $0C45, rfalse $0C50, print $0C55, print_ret $0C87, nop $0C97, save $2064, restore $20FD, restart $1B69, ret_popped $0C9A, pop $0CA8, quit $21BD, new_line $0CAE. Read by $0A34.

The handlers of the sixteen one-operand instructions, opcodes $80-$AF by their low four bits: jz $0CBB, get_sibling $0CC7, get_child $0CD1, get_parent $0CEC, get_prop_len $0CFE, inc $0D21, dec $0D27, print_addr $0D5D, number 8 the illegal-opcode stop $0D6B, remove_obj $0D6E, print_obj $0DD5, ret $0DFF, jump $0E75, print_paddr $0E8B, load $0E9C, not $0EA4. Read by $0A4B.

The handlers of the 25 two-operand instructions, numbers 0-24 from the low five bits of the opcode: 0 the illegal-opcode stop, je $1170, jl $0EB3, jg $0ECB, dec_chk $0EE3, inc_chk $0EF1, jin $0F0F, test $0F1F, or $0F37, and $0F46, test_attr $0F55, set_attr $0F69, clear_attr $0F7E, store $0F97, insert_obj $0FA7, loadw $0FD7, loadb $0FF1, get_prop $100D, get_prop_addr $106E, get_next_prop $10A3, add $10C8, sub $10D8, mul $10E8, div $111D, mod $114F. Read by $0AB8 for both the long form and the variable form.

The handlers of the ten variable-operand instructions, opcodes $E0-$E9: call $11A8, storew $1266, storeb $1291, put_prop $12B4, sread $12EB, print_char $14F0, print_num $14F8, random $1547, push $1566, pull $1574. Read by $0A09.

The top of the Z-machine's instruction loop, where every handler comes back to: it copies the program counter to $F0-$F2, clears the operand count, fetches the opcode ($1752) into $80 and sorts it by its top bits: below $80 a two-operand long form ($0A86), $80-$AF a one-operand short form ($0A4B), $B0-$BF no operands ($0A34), $C0 and up a variable form, whose operand-type byte is read here. The variable form's four 2-bit types give each operand in turn: 00 a word constant ($0AD8), 01 a byte constant ($0ACE), 10 a variable ($0B0B), 11 the end of the operands; each value goes to the next word of $82-$89 and counts in $81. $C0-$DF then go to the two-operand table, $E0-$E9 to the variable-operand table ($0A09).

Picks the handler of a variable-form instruction: $C0-$DF are two-operand instructions in variable form ($0AB8); $E0-$E9 index the table at $098B; $EA-$FF are the illegal-opcode stop. The shared tail at $0A23 reads the handler's address from the table at ($E6) with the index doubled, calls the zero-page hook at $007C (an RTS) and jumps to the handler through $E4.
Picks the handler of an instruction with no operands, $B0-$BB, from the table at $0921; $BC-$BF are the illegal-opcode stop.

Decodes a short-form instruction ($80-$AF): bits 4-5 of the opcode give the operand's type, 00 a word constant, 01 a byte constant, 10 a variable. It stores the value as the first operand, sets the count to 1 and dispatches on the low four bits through the table at $0939.

Decodes a long-form instruction (opcodes below $80): bit 6 says whether the first operand is a byte constant or a variable, bit 5 the same for the second. It stores them as operands 1 and 2, sets the count to 2, and the tail at $0AB8 dispatches on the low five bits through the table at $0959, numbers above 24 being the illegal-opcode stop.
Fetches a one-byte constant operand from the program counter into $E6, with $E7 cleared.
Fetches a two-byte constant operand from the program counter, high byte first, into $E6-$E7.

Reads the variable numbered in A into $E6-$E7 without changing the stack: for variable 0 it pops the top of the Z-machine's stack and pushes it back; any other number goes to $0B12. Used by load, inc and dec, and by the status line for globals 0-2.

Writes $E6-$E7 to the variable numbered in A: for variable 0 it replaces the top of the stack (pop, then push the value) instead of pushing; any other number goes to $0B6C. Used by store, pull, inc and dec.

Fetches a variable operand: reads the variable number from the program counter, and for 0 pops the Z-machine's stack ($1734). Entry $0B12 reads variable A otherwise: 1-15 the local variables at $9A, 16-255 the globals at ($98) + 2(n - 16), each high byte first, into $E6-$E7.
Stores 0 as the instruction's result. $0B4F stores A with a zero high byte, and $0B55 stores $E6-$E7; all three then go back to the instruction loop.

Reads the store byte that follows an instruction and writes $E6-$E7 to that variable: 0 pushes it on the Z-machine's stack ($1708), 1-15 a local, 16-255 a global ($0B6C onwards, which is also the entry for writing variable A).

Ends a test instruction whose condition was true, and $0BB3 one whose condition was false. The branch byte that follows says in bit 7 whether to branch on true or on false; when the condition does not match, the branch bytes are skipped (one or two, by bit 6). When it matches, bit 6 set gives a 6-bit offset, clear a 14-bit signed one with the next byte. An offset of 0 returns false from the routine ($0C50), 1 returns true ($0C45), and anything else moves the program counter by the offset less 2 ($0C02), clearing $8F unless the move is forward within the page.

Adds the signed 16-bit offset in $E6-$E7, less one, to the 17-bit program counter: $8A gets the low byte with its carry, and when the high byte or a carry is non-zero $8B-$8C change too and $8F is cleared so the next fetch looks the page up. The branch code and jump ($0E75) enter here.
rtrue: returns 1 from the current routine, through ret at $0DFF. $0C47 returns the value in A.
rfalse: returns 0 from the current routine.
print: prints the string that follows the instruction in the code, through $0C5B, and goes on after it.

Prints the string at the program counter: it hands the program counter to the data reader ($91-$93), prints the string ($18D2), then takes the address after the string back as the program counter, with the data reader's page pointer and its validity, so the code carries on straight after the text.
print_ret: prints the string that follows, then a carriage return and line feed, and returns 1.
nop: does nothing.
ret_popped: pops the top of the Z-machine's stack and returns it from the routine.
pop: drops the top of the Z-machine's stack.
new_line: prints a carriage return and a line feed ($1B90), which ends the line.
jz: branches if the operand is zero.
get_sibling: stores the object's sibling, byte 5 of its entry, and branches if there is one. The shared tail at $0CD8 does the same for get_child.
get_child: stores the object's first child, byte 6 of its entry, and branches if there is one.
get_parent: stores the object's parent, byte 4 of its entry.
get_prop_len: given the address of a property's data, reads the size byte before it and stores the length, its top three bits plus one.
inc: adds one to the variable numbered by the operand, through $0D2D.
dec: subtracts one from the variable numbered by the operand, through $0D4A.
Adds one to the variable numbered in the first operand and returns the new value in $E6-$E7, for inc and inc_chk. $0D38 writes $E6-$E7 back to the variable for both this and $0D4A.
Subtracts one from the variable numbered in the first operand and returns the new value in $E6-$E7, for dec and dec_chk.
print_addr: prints the string at the byte address given, through the tail of print_paddr at $0E96.
The stop for an opcode the interpreter does not have (1OP number 8, 2OP number 0, and every number past the ends of the tables): JSR $21E7, the fatal error.
remove_obj: takes the object out of the tree ($0D74) and goes back to the instruction loop.

Takes object $82 out of the object tree: if it has a parent, it finds the parent's entry and either makes the object's sibling the parent's first child or walks the siblings until it finds the one before the object and links that one past it; then it clears the object's parent and sibling bytes. The object keeps its own children. Also called by insert_obj.
print_obj: prints the object's short name through $0DDD.

Prints the short name of the object numbered in A: it reads the object's property table address (bytes 7-8 of its entry), skips the length byte and prints the string there. The status line calls it for the room's name.

ret, and the end of every routine: it drops the stack back to the routine's frame, pops the count of locals the call saved and puts the caller's locals back, pops the caller's program counter and frame, and stores the return value (operand 1) in the variable named by the caller's call instruction.
jump: moves the program counter by the signed operand less 2, through $0C02.
print_paddr: prints the string at the packed address given, twice the operand ($17E2). $0E96 prints whatever string the data reader points at and goes back to the instruction loop.
load: stores the value of the variable numbered by the operand; variable 0 reads the top of the stack without popping it.
not: stores the operand with every bit inverted.
jl: branches if the first operand is less than the second, both signed ($16F2), through $0BAA on true and $0BB3 on false. dec_chk and inc_chk end in a copy of the same test, at $0F04.
jg: branches if the first operand is greater than the second, signed: it compares them the other way round.
dec_chk: subtracts one from the variable and branches if the new value is less than the second operand, signed.
inc_chk: adds one to the variable and branches if the new value is greater than the second operand, signed.
jin: branches if the first object's parent is the second operand.
test: branches if every bit set in the second operand is also set in the first.
or: stores the bitwise OR of the two operands.
and: stores the bitwise AND of the two operands.
test_attr: branches if the object has the attribute numbered by the second operand (0-31), found by $163D.
set_attr: sets the object's attribute bit and writes the attribute word back.
clear_attr: clears the object's attribute bit and writes the attribute word back.
store: writes the second operand to the variable numbered by the first; variable 0 replaces the top of the stack. $0FA1 is also pull's way in.
insert_obj: takes the object out of where it is ($0D74), makes the destination its parent, and puts it first among the destination's children, the old first child becoming its sibling.
loadw: stores the word at the array address plus twice the index, read through the data reader so it may be in any page of the story.
loadb: stores the byte at the array address plus the index, read through the data reader.

get_prop: walks the object's property list ($167D) for the property numbered by the second operand. The list is in descending order, so meeting a lower number means the object lacks it, and the value comes from the defaults table at the start of the object table. A one-byte property is stored as it is, a two-byte one as a word; a longer one is the fatal error.
get_prop_addr: stores the story address of the object's property data, or 0 if the object does not have the property.
get_next_prop: stores the number of the property after the one given in the object's list, or of the first when given 0; 0 when the property given is not there or was the last.
add: stores the 16-bit sum of the operands.
sub: stores the first operand less the second.

mul: stores the product. It sets the signs aside ($160F) and fixes the sign after ($161E); a multiplier of 2 or 4 is done with shifts, any other through the general multiply at $157C. The product comes out right even when $160F negates the wrong number, since a 16-bit product wraps the same way whatever the signs. $110C is the shared tail that fixes the sign and stores.

div: stores the quotient, truncated towards zero; a divisor of 2 or 4 is a shift, any other the general divide at $15C1. A negative divisor is never made positive ($160F negates the dividend in its place), so it gives a wrong quotient: run live, 7 / -2, -7 / -2 and 100 / -7 all give 0, while -7 / 2 gives -3 as it should. Nothing tests for a divisor of 0, which gives -1 (live). The story's six divisions divide by 2, 4, 5 or 70, so none of this shows in play.

mod: stores the remainder of the division ($160F, then $15C1). It never fixes the sign afterwards, so a negative dividend gives a positive remainder (live: -7 mod 3 gives 1), and a negative divisor, which $160F leaves negative, gives nonsense: 7 mod -3 gives 32,761 (live), $FFF9 with its top bit lost in $15C1. The story's two uses are a count mod 20 and mod 10, never negative.
je: branches if the first operand equals any of the others (up to three); with fewer than two operands it is the fatal error.

call: calls the routine at the packed address, twice the first operand; a routine address of 0 just stores 0. It pushes the caller's program counter and frame on the Z-machine's stack, reads the new routine's count of locals from its first byte, pushes each old local and fills it with the default the routine gives after the count, then puts the call's other operands into the first locals, pushes the count, and starts the frame here. The new routine runs from the byte after its defaults.

storew: writes the third operand as a word at the array address plus twice the index, high byte first. It writes straight into memory at $2C00 plus the address, so only the resident part of the story can be written.
storeb: writes the low byte of the third operand at the array address plus the index, in the resident part of the story.
put_prop: finds the object's property, which must exist (the fatal error if not), and writes the value into it, a byte or a word by the property's size; a longer property is the fatal error.

sread, the parser's front end: draws the status line ($1CD7), reads a line from the keyboard into the text buffer (first operand, $1D42), then splits it into words in the parse buffer (second operand). A space, question mark, carriage return, line feed, tab or form feed ends a word and is dropped (the list at $13E5); the dictionary's own separators, `,` `.` and `"` in this story, end a word and are words of their own, since the dictionary's list is checked first. Only the first six letters of a word are kept ($13CD skips the rest). Each word is encoded ($1A25) and looked up ($1432), and its entry gets the dictionary address (0 if unknown), its length and its position in the text buffer; the position is written first, as soon as a word begins ($134D). It stops when the line runs out or when the count in byte 1 equals the limit in byte 0 ($131F). The entries are reached through ($84),Y with Y the offset in $E0, so the offset wraps at 256 after the 63rd entry; what that does to a long line is told at the parse buffer, story $2396.
Skips the characters of a word past its sixth, up to the next separator of either kind, so that `lanter` and `lantern` reach the dictionary as the same word.

The eight characters that end a word and are then thrown away: space, full stop, comma, question mark, carriage return, line feed, tab and form feed. The dictionary's own separator list is checked before this one.
Sets the carry if the character in A ends a word: one of the dictionary's separators ($1404) or one of the eight in the table at $13E5 ($13F3, which is also an entry of its own).
Sets the carry if the character in A is one of the eight in the table at $13E5 (space, full stop, comma, question mark, carriage return, line feed, tab, form feed), clears it if not.
Sets the carry if the character in A is in the dictionary's separator list, the bytes at the start of the dictionary ($1419), and clears it otherwise; a zero character is never one.
Puts the memory address of the dictionary, header word 8 plus the story's base, in $E6-$E7.

Looks the encoded word at $DA-$DD up in the dictionary and returns its story address in $E4-$E5, or 0. It skips the separator list, reads the entry length and the count of entries, then strides through the entries sixteen at a time comparing the first byte until it passes the word, steps back one stride, and compares each entry's four bytes in turn. The dictionary is sorted, so it gives up at the first entry greater than the word.
print_char: prints the character whose code is the operand ($1B90).
print_num: prints the operand as a signed decimal number ($1506).

Prints $E6-$E7 as a signed decimal number: a minus sign and the negation first if it is negative ($153F), then the digits, found by dividing by ten again and again and pushing each remainder on the 6502's stack, and printed in the right order as they are pulled; zero prints `0`. The status line uses it for the score and the moves.
Prints a minus sign and makes $E6-$E7 positive ($1625).
random: stores a number from 1 to the operand: the Monitor's keyboard count from $21E8, divided by the operand, the remainder plus one. Nothing deals with an operand of 0 or a negative one.
push: pushes the operand on the Z-machine's stack.
pull: pops the top of the Z-machine's stack into the variable numbered by the operand, through store's tail at $0FA1.
Multiplies $E6-$E7 by $E4-$E5, unsigned, by sixteen rounds of shift and add, and leaves the low 16 bits of the product in $E6-$E7 (the high 16 bits in $E4-$E5). $E8-$E9 are kept.

Divides $E6-$E7 by $E4-$E5, unsigned, by 17 rounds of shift and subtract: the quotient in $E6-$E7 and the remainder in $E4-$E5. $E8-$E9 are kept. A divisor of 0 subtracts nothing each round, so it gives a quotient of $FFFF instead of stopping. The partial remainder is only 16 bits and the last rotate brings in a clear carry, so the remainder comes back with bit 15 clear: one of $8000 or more, possible only when the divisor is over $8000, loses its top bit.

Meant to make $E6-$E7 and $E4-$E5 positive for a multiply or divide, counting in $EA how many were negative: it tests the high byte of each in turn ($1633), but $1633 always negates $E6-$E7, so when the second number is negative it is left as it is and the first is negated instead. A multiply still comes out right, since a 16-bit product wraps the same way whatever the signs; a divide or a remainder by a negative number does not.
Negates the result in $E6-$E7 when an odd number of the operands were negative ($EA bit 0). $1625 negates $E6-$E7 whatever.
If A, a high byte just loaded, is negative: counts it in $EA and negates $E6-$E7, whichever number A came from.

Finds an attribute for test_attr, set_attr and clear_attr: the object's entry ($16BB), the first attribute word for attributes 0-15 or the second for 16-31, the word itself in $E4-$E5 (high byte in $E5) and a mask with the attribute's bit in $E8-$E9, attribute 0 being the top bit of the first byte.

Finds the first property of object $82: the address of its property table from its entry, plus the story's base, in $E6-$E7, and in Y the offset of its first property's size byte, past the short name (twice the name's length in words, plus one).
The number of the property whose size byte is at ($E6),Y: its low five bits.
The size of the property whose size byte is at ($E6),Y, less one: its top three bits.
Moves Y past the property at ($E6),Y to the next one's size byte: the size plus one.

The memory address of the entry of the object numbered in A, in $E6-$E7: nine times the number, plus $35, plus the object table's address (header word $0A) and the story's base. $35 is the 62 bytes of the default property table less one entry, since objects are numbered from 1.

Compares $E6-$E7 with $E4-$E5 as signed numbers and clears the carry when the first is less. When their signs differ the high bytes are compared the other way round; when they agree $16FD compares them unsigned, high bytes then low, and sets Z when they are equal.
Compares $E6-$E7 with $E4-$E5 as unsigned numbers, high bytes first: the carry clear when the first is less, Z set when they are equal. test uses it for its equality, and $16F2 when the signs agree.

Pushes $E6-$E7 on the Z-machine's stack, low byte at the higher address, and counts it; a 179th word is the fatal error. The stack grows down from $03E8, so at its deepest it reaches $0284, inside the line buffer at $0200.
Pops the top of the Z-machine's stack into $E6-$E7; popping more than was pushed is the fatal error.

Fetches the next byte of Z-machine code at the program counter and moves the counter on, crossing pages as it goes. When $8F says the page pointer is stale it finds the page: a resident page is at $2C00 plus the page; any other is looked up in the buffers ($18B5) and marked as used most recently ($1880), or, when no buffer holds it, read from the disk into the oldest buffer ($1E02), whose new page goes in the tables at $2200 and $2280. If the buffer it reuses was the data reader's, the data reader's pointer is marked stale. A disk error restarts the game from $0800.
Points the data reader at the byte address in $E6-$E7, page and offset, and marks its page pointer stale.
Points the data reader at the packed address in $E6-$E7, which it doubles to a 17-bit byte address, for strings: print_paddr and the abbreviations.
Reads a word through the data reader, high byte first, into $E6-$E7.

Reads the next byte through the data reader and moves its address on, in the same way as $1752 does for code: a resident page directly, another through the buffers, read from disk into the oldest buffer when it is not there. If the buffer it reuses holds the program counter's page, the code fetch's pointer is marked stale.

Makes the buffer in A the most recently used: it unlinks it from its place in the two chains of $2300 and $2380 and puts it at the newest end, $BE; if it was the oldest, its newer neighbour becomes the oldest, $BF.
Looks for the page in $E6-$E7 among the buffers' page numbers ($2200 and $2280): found, it returns the buffer in A with the carry clear; not found, the oldest buffer ($BF) with the carry set.

Prints the string the data reader points at: it takes each 5-bit character in turn ($19D9) until the end bit. 0 is a space, 1 an abbreviation, 2 and 3 shift the next character one or two alphabets on, 4 and 5 lock the shift; in alphabet 0, 6-31 are `a`-`z` (the character plus $5B), in alphabet 1 `A`-`Z` (plus $3B), and in alphabet 2 6 starts a character given in full by the next two 5-bit characters, 7 is a new line, and 8-31 come from the table at $19B5.

Prints abbreviation n, the 5-bit character after a 1: the word at entry n of the abbreviation table is a packed address. It saves the alphabet, the decoder's state and the data address on the 6502's stack, prints that string with $18D2, and puts them all back, the shift cleared.
Reduces A to 0-2 by taking 3 away until it is less than 3, for the alphabet arithmetic of the shift characters.

Alphabet 2, the punctuation that 5-bit characters 8-31 stand for after a shift: `0123456789.,!?_#'"/\-:()`. Character 6 starts a 10-bit character and 7 is a new line, so neither is in the table. The word encoder at $1B0B searches it too.
Returns the alphabet for the next character: the single shift if one is pending, which it then cancels, or the locked alphabet.

Returns the next 5-bit character of the string in A with the carry clear, or the carry set at the end. It fetches a new 16-bit word ($17F4) every third character and takes the characters from bits 10-14, 5-9 and 0-4; after the third character of a word with bit 15 set, the string is over.

Encodes the word at $D3-$D8 for the dictionary search: six 5-bit characters at $DA-$DF, padded with 5s. A letter of another alphabet gets a shift lock (4 or 5) when the letter after it is in the same alphabet, a single shift (2 or 3) when it is not; a punctuation mark in alphabet 2 becomes its 5-bit code; any other character becomes a 6 and its code in two 5-bit pieces. When six are written, $1B3C packs them.

Looks for the character in A in the punctuation table at $19B5 and returns its 5-bit code, its place plus 8, with Z clear, or Z set when it is not there. The search starts at place $24, thirteen bytes past the end of the 24 characters, in the code that follows the table, so a character equal to one of those bytes, such as a backtick ($60), gets a code too big for five bits.
Which alphabet the character in A belongs to: 0 for `a`-`z`, 1 for `A`-`Z`, 2 for anything else; a zero byte gives 0, and a byte with bit 7 set comes back as it was, which the parser never passes it.
Packs the six 5-bit characters at $DA-$DF into two 16-bit words, low byte first at $DA-$DB and $DC-$DD, three characters to a word, and sets the end bit on the second.
restart: ends the line on the screen and starts the interpreter again from $0800, which reads the story's resident part from the disk afresh.

Finds the top page of RAM: from $BF downwards it tests one byte of each page, reading it twice and writing its complement, until it finds one that holds what was written, and puts the byte back. It returns the page in A: $BF on a machine with 48K or more, $7F with 32K.

Puts one character into the output line at $0200: a carriage return shows the line ($1C5B); other control characters are dropped; lower case is turned into capitals, since the Apple II and II+ have none; bit 7 is set for the screen. When the line passes the window's width it is broken at the last space ($1BB5), shown, and the rest moved to the start of a new line.

Breaks the output line that has run past the window's width: it looks back from the end for a space, or breaks at the width if there is none, shows the line up to the break ($1C5B), and copies the characters after the break to the start of the buffer.
Sends the output line waiting at $0200 to the printer when header byte $11 has bit 0 set (SCRIPT is on, $1BF2), then to the screen ($1C40).
Set to 1 once the printer card has been sent its set-up string ($1C07); 0 until the first line is printed.

Sends the output line to the printer: it puts the printer hook ($EE-$EF, slot 1) in CSW and prints each character through COUT, then puts the screen's hook back, keeping whatever the card left in CSW for next time. The first time, it sends CONTROL-I and `80N`, a command string for the printer card in slot 1, and puts $91 in $0779, a screen hole that belongs to slot 1; what the card makes of them is the card's business and was not checked.
Shows the output line at $0200 on the screen through COUT1 and empties it.
The text `[MORE]`, shown in inverse at the bottom of the screen by $1C5B.

Ends the output line and counts it: when the lines printed since the last input fill the window, it shows `[MORE]` in inverse, waits for a key (RDKEY), rubs the prompt out and starts the count again. Then it shows the line ($1BE2) and prints a carriage return unless the line filled the width, when the screen has already moved to the next line; with SCRIPT on, the printer gets a carriage return too.
Clears the text window (HOME), leaving the status line, and restarts the count of lines.
The text `SCORE:`, printed on the status line by $1CD7.

Draws the status line on row 0 before each input: it sets the inverse flag and clears the row with CLREOL, which leaves normal spaces (the snapshots' row 0), then prints in inverse the short name of the object in global 0 (the room) at column 0, `SCORE:` at column 25, then global 1 (the score), a slash and global 2 (the moves), and puts the cursor back where it was.
Prints X characters from ($E6) on the screen through COUT1 with bit 7 set, for the texts of [MORE], the status line and the save prompts.

Reads the player's line into the text buffer at ($82): it shows any waiting output, reads it into $0200 with the Monitor's GETLN1, where the left arrow rubs out and RETURN ends the line, puts a carriage return at the end, prints the line on the printer when SCRIPT is on, and copies it into the text buffer from byte 1, capitals turned to lower case, no more than the buffer's size (byte 0) and stopping at the carriage return. It returns the count of characters copied.

Sets the screen up for the game: the text window from row 1 to 24, the full 40 columns, so that row 0 stays the status line; the Monitor's prompt character `>`; normal video; then clears the window ($1CC9).

The parameter block for the disk routines at $2900, in the layout of DOS 3.3's IOB: $1DAC the table type 1, $1DAD the slot times 16 ($60, slot 6, changed by the save prompts), $1DAE the drive (1, or the save drive), $1DAF the volume, 0 for any, $1DB0 the track, $1DB1 the sector, $1DB2-$1DB3 the address of the device characteristics table ($1DBD), $1DB4-$1DB5 the buffer's address, $1DB7 the byte count (0 for 256), $1DB8 the command (1 read, 2 write), $1DB9 the error code returned, $1DBA-$1DBC the volume, slot and drive of the last access.
The parameter block's slot times 16: $60 for the game disk in slot 6, set from the slot answer before a save or a restore ($1F0E) and back to $60 after ($2059).
The parameter block's drive: 1 for the game disk, the drive answer before a save or a restore ($1F2B), and 1 again after ($205E).
The parameter block's track, worked out from the page number by $1DCE.
The parameter block's sector, the remainder left by $1DD3's division of the page number by 16.
The low byte of the parameter block's buffer address, from $E6 at $1DC4.
The high byte of the parameter block's buffer address, from $E7 at $1DC9.
The parameter block's command: 1 to read and 2 to write, stored by $1DC1 for each sector.
The device characteristics table the parameter block names: 0 a Disk II, 1 phase to a track, and the motor's start-up count $EFD8, of which the disk routines use the $D8.
The third byte of the device characteristics table, $EF, which the disk routines do not read; $1E08 saves and rewrites it round each write.
The fourth byte of the device characteristics table, $D8, which the disk routines read as the high byte of the motor's start-up count ($2960).

Reads (A = 1) or writes (A = 2) one sector through the disk routines: page $E4-$E5 of the story or the saved game, at the address in $E6-$E7. The page number becomes track 3 plus the page divided by 16 ($7F) and sector the remainder, so the story starts on track 3 and a saved game on track 3 plus four for each position. It returns the disk routines' carry, set on an error.

Reads the next sector of a saved game into the buffer at $0200: page $E4-$E5 plus one. $1DFC reads into the address already in $E6-$E7, and $1E02 reads page $E4-$E5 itself, the entry the story's paging uses.
Reads the next sector of a saved game into the page at $E6-$E7: restore calls it for each page of the story's dynamic memory.

Reads page $E4-$E5 of the story from the game disk into the page at $E6-$E7, through $1DC1 with command 1; the carry comes back set on a disk error. The start-up code and the paging of code and data call it.

Writes the next sector of a saved game from the buffer at $0200: page $E4-$E5 plus one. $1E10 writes from the address already in $E6-$E7. It puts $EF and $D8 into the device characteristics table for the write and the old bytes back after, which with this table's bytes changes nothing.

Writes the next sector of a saved game from the page at $E6-$E7, not the buffer: save calls it for each page of the story's dynamic memory, with the device characteristics table's bytes put back after.
Sets the screen up at start-up, through $1D90.
Prints X characters from ($E6) through the output line ($1B90), for the save and restore prompts and the end of the session.

The save and restore prompts, in one block: `PLEASE INSERT SAVE DISKETTE,` (28 characters), then at $1E6A a byte the prompts use as a variable, the offset of the question being asked (0, $10 or $20), then three questions of fifteen characters each followed by its default answer: `SLOT     (1-7):` and `6`, `DRIVE    (1-2):` and `2`, `POSITION (0-7):` and `0`; then `DEFAULT = ` and `--- PRESS 'RETURN' KEY TO BEGIN ---`. The player's answer is written over the default, so the next save offers the same position, slot and drive.

A variable inside the prompt text: the offset from $1E6B of the save question being asked, 0 for the slot, $10 for the drive, $20 for the position, set by $1EC8 before each call of $1F6F. The fifteen characters after it are the first question, `SLOT     (1-7):`.
The default answer to the slot question, `6` at first and afterwards the last slot given (written at $1F12); the fifteen characters after it are the second question, `DRIVE    (1-2):`.
The default answer to the drive question, `2` at first and afterwards the last drive given (written at $1F2F); the fifteen characters after it are the third question, `POSITION (0-7):`.

The default answer to the position question, `0` at first and afterwards the last position given (written at $1EF1; $1F55 reads it to find the position's first sector). After it come `DEFAULT = ` and `--- PRESS 'RETURN' KEY TO BEGIN ---`.

The questions SAVE and RESTORE both ask, as the reference card gives them: it clears the screen, asks for the save diskette, then the position (0-7), the slot (1-7) and the drive (1-2), each with its default ($1F6F) and each refused and asked again when out of range, and sets the parameter block's slot and drive from the answers. It waits for RETURN, and returns in $E4-$E5 the page before the position's first sector, 64 pages to a position.

Asks one of the save questions: it prints the question at offset $1E6A, `DEFAULT = ` and the default answer in inverse at column 25, waits for a key, rubs the default out, and returns the key, or the default when the key is RETURN, with bit 7 clear.
`PLEASE RE-INSERT GAME DISKETTE,`, 31 characters, the first of the two lines $201E prints after a save or restore that used the game's own drive ($202F-$2039).
`--- PRESS 'RETURN' KEY TO CONTINUE ---`, 38 characters, the second line, printed at $203F-$2049 before the wait for RETURN.
The last 30 characters of the line at $1FF8, `S 'RETURN' KEY TO CONTINUE ---`, which run on past $2000.

After a save or a restore: when the save diskette was in the game's own drive (slot 6, drive 1), it asks for the game diskette back and waits for RETURN; then it sets the parameter block back to slot 6, drive 1, where the story is read from.

save: asks the save questions ($1EC8), then writes the game's state to four tracks of the save diskette from the first sector of the position chosen. The first sector holds the story's version byte, the program counter, the fifteen locals and the stack's count, pointer and frame; the next two hold the Z-machine's stack area $0280-$03E7; then come the story's pages from 0 up to the one after the page where its dynamic memory ends (header byte $0E), 46 pages with this story, one more than restore reads back. Each block is copied backwards into the buffer at $0200. It branches on success, after asking for the game diskette back ($201E).
Copies Y bytes from ($E6) into the buffer at $0200 from offset X, the last byte first, so the block arrives reversed; restore reverses it back ($219D).

restore: asks the save questions, reads the position's first sector and checks that its first byte is this story's version; then it puts back the program counter, locals and stack, the stack area and the dynamic memory, keeping the header's byte $11 (the SCRIPT flag) as it is now. It branches on success, after asking for the game diskette back; a disk error or a version that does not match is a failure.
Copies Y bytes from the buffer at $0200, offset X, to ($E6), the last byte first, undoing the reversal of $20F1.
The text `-- END OF SESSION --`, which quit prints.
quit: prints `-- END OF SESSION --` and stops in a loop that jumps to itself, until the player switches off or resets.
The text `ZORK INTERNAL ERROR!`. Nothing in the interpreter refers to it: the fatal error is a BRK ($21E7), which leaves the player at the Monitor's prompt instead.

The interpreter's one fatal error: a BRK, which stops the game and drops into the Monitor. Called for a header it cannot run, an illegal opcode, je with one operand, a property get_prop or put_prop cannot handle, and a Z-machine stack that overflows or underflows.

Returns the Monitor's keyboard count RNDL-RNDH ($4E-$4F) in $E6-$E7, rotating the high byte left first so that two calls in one turn differ. The count runs while the Monitor waits for a key, so the game's random numbers come from the player's typing speed.
Thirteen bytes after the interpreter's last routine that nothing reads: the interpreter's tables begin at $2200, and the loader's code that ran there is gone.

Splits the 256-byte sector at ($3E) into the 342 six-bit values a write puts on the disk: the top six bits of each byte go to $2700-$27FF, and the bottom two bits of three bytes at a time are gathered into the 86 bytes of $2800-$2855.

Writes the sector held at $2700-$2855 into the data field that follows the address field just read: it checks the disk is not write-protected (the carry comes back set if it is), writes five sync bytes, the prologue D5 AA BC, the 342 nibbles each the EOR of a six-bit value and the one before, translated through the table at $2629, a checksum nibble, and the epilogue DE AA EB FF. Where DOS 3.3 writes D5 AA AD, this writes D5 AA BC, so a saved game's sectors carry the same prologue as the game disk's.

Writes the nibble in A to the disk in the slot in X, taking the 32 cycles a nibble lasts: $24B8 clears the carry first, and $24B9 and $24BB enter later for nibbles that follow code that has already used some of the cycles.
The write-a-nibble routine entered after its CLC, so with the carry as the caller left it.
The write-a-nibble routine entered at the store itself, seven cycles later than $24B9, for a nibble whose timing the caller has already used up.

Puts a sector read into $2700-$2855 back together as bytes at ($3E): each byte is a six-bit value from $2700 with two more bits taken from the right byte of $2800. Stops at the count in $26 (0 for all 256).

Reads the data field after an address field: it waits for D5 AA BC within 32 nibbles, reads 342 nibbles, undoing the EOR chain through the table at $2696 into $2800 and $2700, then the checksum nibble and the epilogue DE AA. It returns the carry clear when all is well, set on any mismatch; a DOS 3.3 data field, D5 AA AD, does not read.

Finds and reads the next address field: D5 AA 96 within about 770 nibbles, then the volume, track, sector and checksum, each from two 4-and-4 nibbles, into $2F, $2E, $2D and $2C, then the epilogue DE AA. The carry is clear when all is well and the checksum agrees, set otherwise.

Moves the head of the drive in the slot in X to the half-track position in A, one step at a time from the position kept in $0478, speeding up and slowing down with the times in the tables at $2611 and $261D, and turning each phase magnet on and off ($25EE).

Turns a phase magnet on (carry set) or off (carry clear): $25EE for the head position kept in $0478, $25F1 for the position in A. It reads the switch at $C080 plus twice the phase plus the carry, offset by the slot.
Turns the phase magnet for the head position in A on or off by the carry; the second entry of the routine at $25EE.
Three bytes between the head-moving code and the delay routine, $AA $A0 $A0, that nothing reads.
Waits for about A times 100 microseconds, counting up the 16-bit motor timer at $46 as it goes, so that the drive's start-up time passes while the head moves.
Twelve delays, one for each step of a head movement, with the step's magnet on: long at first, shorter as the head picks up speed ($25D4).
Twelve delays with the step's magnet off, used with $2611 for each step ($25E0).
The 64 disk nibbles, $96 to $FF with gaps, that the 64 six-bit values become when written: value n is the byte at $2629 + n. Each has its top bit set, as every byte on the disk must.

45 bytes between the write table and the read table. The write routine's index stops at $3F, and the read routine, which reads $2600 plus the nibble, would reach $2680-$2695 only for a nibble below $96, which is no valid nibble; nothing else reads them.

The read routine's decoding table, read as $2600 plus the nibble, for nibbles $96-$FF: each of the 64 valid nibbles gives back its six-bit value, 0-$3F, at its own place. The places between hold bytes no valid nibble reaches.

For the format routine: writes a run of sync bytes (the count in Y), then an address field for the sector in $3F, the track in $44 and the volume in $41, in 4-and-4 nibbles with the checksum, between D5 AA 96 and DE AA EB. The carry comes back set if the disk is write-protected.
Writes the byte in A as two 4-and-4 nibbles, the odd bits and then the even ones, each ORed with $AA, for the address field.
Writes the nibble in A after a delay of a few cycles (the NOPs before $28D8 make up the 32 cycles a nibble takes), for the address field's bytes; $28D5 enters one NOP later.
The write of a nibble in A for the address field, entered one cycle-pair later than $28D4.
33 bytes before the disk routines' entry that nothing reads.

The disk routines' entry, the interpreter's only way to the disk: Y and A give the parameter block, which is always $1DAC. It selects the slot and drive, waits for the motor if it was off, moves the head to the track asked for and finds the sector by its address field, translating the sector number through the table at $2BB8. It retries: it seeks again when it lands on the wrong track, takes the head back to track 0 when 48 tries find no good sector, and gives up after the second time. Then it reads, writes or formats according to the block's command byte (1, 2 or 4; 0 only seeks), stores the error code in the block's byte $0D and returns the carry set on an error: $10 write-protected, $20 the wrong volume, $40 when the sector could not be found or read.

Moves the selected drive's head to the track in A: it doubles the track to a half-track position when the device characteristics table says one phase to a track, keeps each drive's position in its own screen hole ($0478 or $04F8 plus the slot), and seeks ($25A0).
Turns the slot times 16 in X into the slot number in Y, to index the screen holes.
Records the track position in A as the current one for the drive in the parameter block, in $0478 or $04F8 plus the slot.

Formats a disk: from track 0 to 34 it writes sixteen sectors of empty data ($2B0D), then reads the track back, and stops with error $08 if it will not read. The interpreter has no command that calls it: the parameter block's command byte is only ever 1 or 2.

Writes one track for the format routine: sixteen address fields, each followed by an empty data field, with $45 sync bytes before each, then reads the track back until every sector has been seen once, marking each in the table at $2BA8, and adjusts the sync count so that the next track fits.
An RTS that the format routine calls three times in a row as a delay ($2B3A-$2B40), and that its error branches at $2B1A and $2B1F reach to return with the carry set.

Sixteen bytes, one for each sector, for the format routine: it fills them with $30 at the start of each track ($2B2D-$2B36) and puts $FF in a sector's byte when that sector reads back ($2B8F). The $FF in the snapshot came with the disk's track 0; the format routine never runs.

The order in which the disk routines find a page's sectors: logical sector n is the physical sector given here, 0, 4, 8, 12, 1, 5, 9, 13, 2, 6, 10, 14, 3, 7, 11, 15, so consecutive pages of the story lie four sectors apart round a track.

56 bytes that nothing runs or reads: the code map from the Z-machine's start through play, saving and restoring never reached them, and no instruction refers to them. As instructions they would switch the language card's RAM in for writing, store 0 at $E000 and jump to $2344, inside the loader the interpreter's tables have overwritten; the bytes from $2BD9 decode as more fragments that no code reaches. They are typed as bytes so that the disassembler does not follow them.
